Empirical Research Plan – Trade Liberalization and Wages in Developing Countries
=====================================================================

1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study extension, exploiting cross-industry variation in the size of tariff reductions that occurs at a common national reform date.

Why it fits  
• We have a panel of industries observed before and after a discrete, externally imposed policy shock (trade–liberalization package).  
• Industries differ markedly in pre-reform tariff levels; hence the magnitude of the tariff cut varies quasi-exogenously across sectors.  
• DID leverages these two dimensions (time × industry) to net out common macro shocks while attributing differential wage changes to differential trade exposure.  
• Event-study leads/lags allow us to visualize pre-trends and dynamic adjustment.

2. Treatment and Control
------------------------
Treatment variable  
Option A (Binary): Treated_i = 1 if the industry’s cumulative tariff drop between t₀-1 and t₀+2 lies above the median (or a policy-relevant threshold, e.g., >10 pp).  
Option B (Preferred, Continuous): ΔTariff_it = (Tariff_it – Tariff_i,t-1) or cumulative ΔTariff_i post-reform. We interpret the coefficient as the semi-elasticity of wages with respect to tariffs.

Control group  
Industries experiencing small or no tariff change (bottom quartile) serve as the control in the binary setup; in the continuous setup, identification arises from differential intensity, so all industries contribute (weight proportional to their change).

Treatment timing  
t₀ = first year in which the new tariff schedule becomes effective (e.g., 1995 if reform legislated in late 1994). Leads (t<0) and lags (t>0) of ΔTariff will be coded for event-study.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent the reform, high-cut and low-cut industries would have followed similar wage trajectories.  
  – Plausibility: macro environment (inflation, exchange rates) affects all industries; we can inspect pre-reform trends and include industry-specific linear trends.

A2. Exogeneity of tariff reductions conditional on pre-reform levels: The size of the cut is driven by political economy and WTO negotiations, not by contemporaneous, unobserved shocks to wages.  
  – Plausibility: reform was part of a package negotiated at national level; industries rarely lobby successfully for idiosyncratic deviations once schedule is locked.

A3. No anticipatory wage adjustment: Firms could not fully re-contract wages before t₀ in expectation of the cut.  
  – Plausibility: Implementation dates sometimes uncertain; will test by including 2–3 pre-period leads.

A4. Stable composition: Industry coding and employment measurement remain consistent; no massive post-reform reclassification.  
  – Plausibility: Manufacturing classification (ISIC 3-digit) stable; we will check entry/exit patterns.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
-------------------------------------------
T1. Concurrent reforms (e.g., privatization, exchange-rate devaluation)  
  • Mitigation: Add country–year fixed effects (or macro controls if single-country), interact them with broad sector dummies, and show that results survive.

T2. Selective industry exit or entry (survivorship bias)  
  • Mitigation: Use balanced panel where possible; alternatively, weight by pre-reform employment and implement inverse-probability reweighting for attrition.

T3. Measurement error in tariffs (ad-valorem vs. specific, applied vs. MFN)  
  • Mitigation: Cross-verify with WTO/UNCTAD TRAINS; instrument ΔAppliedTariff with ΔStatutoryTariff (least‐squares attenuation check).

5. R Code Outline
-----------------
```r
# --- 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data wrangling
library(fixest)       # high-performance FE regressions
library(modelsummary) # nice tables

# --- 1. Data Loading ---------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("industry_panel.csv")  # assume one row per ind-year

# --- 2. Variable Construction -----------------------------------
# Log real wages (firm-weighted industry average)
dt[, ln_wage := log(real_wage)]

# Tariff change: first difference
setorder(dt, industry_id, year)
dt[, d_tariff := tariff - shift(tariff, 1L, type = "lag"), by = industry_id]

# Reform indicator (t0 = 1995 in this illustration)
reform_year <- 1995
dt[, post := as.integer(year >= reform_year)]

# Above-median tariff cut (binary treatment)
cut_size <- dt[year == reform_year, .(cum_cut = shift(tariff, 1L) - tariff), by = industry_id]
median_cut <- median(cut_size$cum_cut, na.rm = TRUE)
dt <- merge(dt, cut_size, by = "industry_id", all.x = TRUE)
dt[, treated := as.integer(cum_cut > median_cut)]

# Event-study leads/lags
for (k in -4:6){
  dt[, paste0("leadlag_", k) := as.integer(year - reform_year == k) * d_tariff]
}

# --- 3. Main DID Regression -------------------------------------
# Continuous treatment specification
did_main <- feols(ln_wage ~ post * d_tariff | industry_id + year,
                  data = dt, cluster = ~industry_id)
etable(did_main, title = "Main DID: Wage response to tariff change")

# Binary high-vs-low cut DID
did_bin  <- feols(ln_wage ~ post * treated | industry_id + year,
                  data = dt, cluster = ~industry_id)

# Event-study (dynamic effects)
lag_vars <- paste0("leadlag_", -4:6)[-5]  # drop k = -1 to be baseline
event_mod <- feols(ln_wage ~ .SD | industry_id + year,
                   data = dt, cluster = ~industry_id,
                   .SDcols = lag_vars)

# --- 4. Robustness: Pre-trend placebo window (-6:-2) -------------
placebo <- feols(ln_wage ~ d_tariff | industry_id + year,
                 data = dt[year %between% c(reform_year-6, reform_year-2)],
                 cluster = ~industry_id)
```

6. Expected Results
-------------------
Theory (Stolper-Samuelson) predicts that reducing import tariffs lowers the relative wage of workers employed in import-competing sectors in labor-abundant (developing) countries, but may raise wages overall if the country’s abundant factor (labor) gains from export expansion. With industry-level data we expect:  
• A 10 percentage-point tariff cut in an import-competing industry lowers its average real wage by roughly 2–4 %.  
• Heterogeneity: export-oriented industries could see neutral or mildly positive effects.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
-------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically supported …… 0.8  
C2: No spillovers across industries (limited worker mobility) … 0.6  
C3: Stable treatment assignment (tariffs not reversed) ………… 1.0  
C4: No differential attrition/reclassification …………………… 0.7  
C5: Common shocks absorbed by fixed effects …………………… 0.9  

Average ≈ 0.8 – overall reasonably strong but still reliant on pre-trend evidence and robustness exercises.

End of Plan
